posts.title: A Dutch court has temporarily banned Chinese electric vehicle manufacturer BYD from selling, manufacturing and importing its seven-seat Ti7 SUV across the European Union after ruli
posts.author: Bloom Pakistan
posts.snippet:
A Dutch court has temporarily banned Chinese electric vehicle manufacturer BYD from selling, manufacturing and importing its seven-seat Ti7 SUV across the European Union after ruling that the vehicle infringes Jaguar Land Rover’s (JLR) registered design rights for the iconic Land Rover Defender.

The District Court of The Hague issued the preliminary injunction on November 20, finding that the BYD Ti7 shares distinctive exterior design features with the current-generation Land Rover Defender 110, including its boxy silhouette, rounded body shoulders, distinctive wheel arches and rear-side body panel.

The court concluded that the differences highlighted by BYD were insufficient to create a substantially different overall visual impression.
The ruling follows legal action by Jaguar Land Rover, which is owned by India’s Tata Motors, over alleged similarities between the two SUVs.

BYD to Appeal Dutch Court Decision
BYD has strongly rejected the court’s findings, maintaining that the Ti7 was developed through its own independent design process and does not infringe any of Jaguar Land Rover’s intellectual property rights.
The Chinese automaker has announced plans to appeal the decision. The European sales restrictions will remain in place unless the appeal succeeds.
According to reports, the injunction covers importing, manufacturing, offering for sale, selling, storing and delivering the Ti7 across the European Union. Violating the order could result in penalties of up to €100,000 per day, capped at €10 million.

UK Launch Not Affected by European Ban
Importantly, the Dutch court’s decision does not prevent BYD from launching the Ti7 in the United Kingdom.

The court declined to extend the injunction to Britain, citing jurisdictional limitations concerning BYD’s UK subsidiary and rejecting JLR’s claims under UK design rights in these proceedings.
The seven-seat SUV is scheduled to begin customer deliveries in the UK in January 2027.

Although the Ti7 has not yet officially entered the EU market, the court considered BYD’s promotional activities and statements about its European development plans sufficient to establish a potential risk of future design infringement.

posts.title: Messaging standards. What's up?
posts.author: Clemens Vasters
posts.snippet:
Messaging standards. What's up?

There's a collaborative spirit in the messaging space these days. There used to be times when people from, say, IBM and Microsoft would not be in the same room without lawyers present, but luckily we are *really* over that now.

Some noteworthy things that are going on:
- OASIS AMQP TC regrouped with a new constellation of collaborators, first public review drafts for JSPN-RPC 2.0 over AMQP and Model Context Protocol over AMQP published
- One reference/demo code base for MCP over AMQP for Rabbit MQ, Artemis, ActiveMQ, Azure Service Bus, and IBM MQ
- RabbitMQ, ActiveMQ, Artemis, Qpid, and Azure Service Bus share a single provider implementation for JMS 2.0 over AMQP 
- OASIS MQTT TC pushing ahead with MQTT-SN and MQTT over QUIC work.
- Agreement to form a joint (!) AMQP & MQTT subcommittee for message-level encryption and integrity with existing input spec
- CNCF xRegistry metadata system very close to the v1.0 finish line with a "capital S standardization" path into a formal standards body being finalized with the Linux Foundation at this time (latter also for CNCF CloudEvents).
- OPC Foundation eyeing xRegistry and CloudEvents in combination with MQTT
- JSON Structure in IETF is picking up a bit of a fan base

In the xRegistry project, for right after the v1.0 release, we have queued up working drafts for registries for Omniverse USD, Web Of Things, API definitions, and media streaming endpoints. 

In early 2027, I'll bring a proposal for contract/choreography model to OASIS that spans APIs and asynchronous communication and is explicitly designed to cover Agent-to-Agent (inside backend systems) and "human-in-the-loop" in addition to classic "service oriented" distributed system data and control flow exchanges. Some industry folks have seen it and gave encouraging feedback, but due to intellectual property rules, I can only share this publicly once the venue is settled. There and many composite scenarios where HTTP, AMQP, MQTT, Kafka RPC, and media transfer protocols can each play out their strengths for particular communication paths, and my personal goal is to enable users (and coding agents) to choose the best tool for the job in an overarching interoperability and metadata context.

posts.title: Tokenised money market funds and the EU’s regulatory framework — PwC & EFAMA
posts.author: Olaf Ammermann
posts.snippet:
Tokenised money market funds and the EU’s regulatory framework — PwC & EFAMA

"Tokenised MMFs are already scaling commercially. Global tMMF market capitalisation is estimated at around EUR 7 billion and has roughly doubled in a year (outpacing both stablecoins and traditional MMFs), with EU-domiciled products at approximately EUR 725 million. Major asset managers and crypto-native firms have launched products, demonstrating that existing EU frameworks (MMFR, UCITS, MiFID, MiCAR + CAFI Guidelines) can already accommodate tokenised structures. 

The clearest near-term value is as programmable collateral. Direct transfer of tMMF units as collateral (without the current inefficient “round-trip” redemption-to-cash process) could unlock real-time margin posting, automatic substitution and atomic delivery-versus-payment. Recognition of tMMF units as eligible HQLA under EMIR is where tokenisation benefits are most tangible. 

The MMF Regulation is already technology-neutral. It defines an MMF by investment objective rather than by the form in which units are issued or the register is maintained, so tokenised structures fall squarely within the existing framework without any need for amendment. 

Funds should be expressly permitted to hold and accept stablecoins. Regulated funds (including tMMFs) should be allowed to hold and accept stablecoins for subscription and redemption purposes, as well as for settlement of portfolio assets, gas fees and other ancillary costs. This should build on the approach already taken by the CSSF and AMF and be harmonised across all Member States. 

Some targeted regulatory changes would improve the DLT use case for collateral. The Financial Collateral Directive should confirm that DLT-based assets are in scope and provide greater certainty on how “possession” and “control” are established. Tokenised MMFs should also be expressly confirmed as eligible collateral under the EMIR regulatory technical standards, on the same technology-neutral terms as their non-tokenised equivalents. Classification between MiFID and MiCAR is clear, with only residual edge cases remaining.

Settlement finality must be clarified for DLT systems. Converting the Settlement Finality Directive into a directly applicable Settlement Finality Regulation (as proposed in the Market Integration and Supervision Package) would establish a technology-neutral framework that explicitly accommodates DLT, with harmonised finality definitions and an ESMA transparency database."

Can you legally hold or trade cryptocurrency where you live without risking fines or freezes? 

The answer is rarely a simple yes or no. Cryptocurrency legality depends on nuanced national laws, regulatory frameworks, and ongoing government actions. Many confuse legality with regulation: something can be legal but strictly regulated, requiring compliance steps to avoid penalties. Others assume crypto is outright banned if unregulated, which is often incorrect.

Navigating these complex waters means understanding the exact legal status in your jurisdiction, how regulators classify tokens, and what licenses or disclosures are mandated. Without this clarity, businesses and investors can face unexpected legal risks that stall growth or trigger enforcement.

posts.title: What's one man's private life worth? For NVIDIA, apparently about US$1 trillion.
posts.author: Ervin Jenn Farn Loke
posts.snippet:
What's one man's private life worth? For NVIDIA, apparently about US$1 trillion.

It lost more than that while Jensen Huang was gone, and won back US$952 billion the day he returned.

On 12 November, Huang stepped down as CEO after reports of two affairs, one of them with a woman alleged to have links to Chinese intelligence. By the next Friday, Nvidia's shares were down 28%. On Monday the board reinstated him. Nvidia had its best day since 2003 (+31.5%) and the Nasdaq rose 6.5%.

The odd part: on 17 November, under an interim CEO, Nvidia reported quarterly revenue of US$115.8 billion, up 103% on a year ago. The shares kept falling. 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐦𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐭 𝐰𝐚𝐬 𝐩𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐨𝐧𝐞 𝐦𝐚𝐧, 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐜𝐡𝐢𝐩𝐬 𝐜𝐚𝐦𝐞 𝐬𝐞𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐝.

1. 𝐖𝐡𝐨 𝐝𝐞𝐜𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐬 𝐰𝐡𝐨 𝐫𝐮𝐧𝐬 𝐚 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐚𝐧𝐲 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐠𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐧𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐝𝐨𝐞𝐬𝐧'𝐭 𝐨𝐰𝐧?
The board said it acted after "input from senior levels of the United States government". The President was less subtle: "I spoke to them, let me just put it that way, and I convinced them." Later: "basically I was represented at the board."

I'm not a lawyer. Governance experts are split, and so far nobody has shown a law was broken. That's what worries me. If it's legal, it's a precedent: any company big enough to move the index now has an unofficial shareholder in the White House.

That backing also shields the board: a president has vouched that Huang is no security risk. But a shield one administration hands you can become a lever for the next.

2. 𝐖𝐡𝐞𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐂𝐄𝐎 𝐢𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐛𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐝
Tony Fernandes and AirAsia. Elon Musk and Tesla. Jeff Bezos and Amazon. Bernard Arnault and LVMH. Jensen Huang and his leather jacket.

A founder people recognise does the work of an ad budget and an influencer roster at once. Tesla went years without a traditional ad campaign because Musk's feed did the job.
I do marketing at Accomy, a corporate travel startup, and this is the trade-off I think about most. A CEO's voice is the cheapest channel a young company has.

The catch is that it comes as a bundle. The founder's personality, opinions, tone and private life all become part of the product, and you don't get to choose which part the market reacts to. This month Nvidia's value swung on its CEO's personal life while its products stayed the same.

3. 𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐈 𝐬𝐞𝐞 𝐍𝐯𝐢𝐝𝐢𝐚
I think Huang is still the right person to lead it. He co-founded the company in 1993 and has run it for 33 years, through a near-bankruptcy, gaming, crypto and now AI. You can't hire that kind of commitment. Its revenue and its moat in chips and software don't leave when one person does.

These 11 days exposed a risk no balance sheet lists. One man's private life moved a trillion dollars in each direction, and a president helped decide who runs the company.

posts.title: Have you heard about COP31?
posts.author: Ivana Cattafi
posts.snippet:
Have you heard about COP31?
And one question: Who isn't feeling the heat in Malta this November?
For those unfamiliar, COP is the UN's annual climate summit, where nearly 200 countries negotiate how to tackle climate change.

What went wrong?
Countries failed to reach agreement on key political issues, particularly the transition away from fossil fuels and climate finance: who pays, how much, and how fast we act.

What's next?
COP32 is scheduled for 2027 in Ethiopia. Meanwhile, climate change isn't waiting for another summit.

My biggest takeaway?
Perhaps climate action needs a better lawyer.
Because what good are commitments if accountability and enforcement are not strong enough to turn them into action?
Nature doesn't negotiate. It doesn't wait for political consensus or accept extensions.
We can negotiate the terms of the transition, but we cannot negotiate with the laws of nature.

Climate change is no longer a distant prediction. It is becoming part of our everyday reality.

Introducing DeNeuvella – A Platform for Strategic Human Capital Capabilities, Transformation, and Analytics

Every organization is in a constant state of change, and with it, the skill requirements for various roles within the workforce evolve. While companies often employ data-driven planning—utilizing ERP and HR systems to track employee skills—a gap frequently persists between these systems and the broader strategic direction of the business. DeNeuvella exists to bridge this gap within the organization.

DeNeuvella identifies the skills of individual employees, aligns them with the requirements of specific job families, and organizes them into "Capability Cluster Bands." When a project necessitates a transformation or a shift in roles, the platform identifies the affected employees and suggests suitable new placements—complete with a "match percentage" and the specific training required.

Transformation Projects: Designed for both company-wide initiatives and specific teams under individual managers.
Capability Cluster Bands and a redeployment engine.
AI Agents: For data validation, skill mapping, and skill gap analysis.
"Ask the Platform": An AI-powered chat interface that serves as a guide for using the platform while providing access to corporate documentation.
Workforce Analytics: Includes 120 templates covering 8 dimensions of the workforce.

posts.title: Return of the Huang
posts.author: Kok Liang CHEW
posts.snippet:
Return of the Huang
  
Nearly $1 trillion added in one day. One White House intervention. Corporate governance blinked?
  
On 17 Nov 2026, NVIDIA’s board ruled out reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO and hired head-hunters for a fresh direction. Six days later, 23 Nov 2026, it reversed course unanimously after President Trump lobbied directors.
  
The Financial Times estimates Trump’s disclosed NVIDIA shares jumped up to $15 million on paper in that rally. Now, let’s look at the precedent set.
  
Huang resigned 11 days earlier after admitting an affair tied to Alice Huang, an alleged Chinese spy whose former firm, Megaspeed, Washington blacklisted on 23 Nov 2026. Reports also revealed affairs with NVIDIA staff, plus more disclosed to the board.
  
“He's not the Messiah; he's a very naughty boy!"
  
CEOs at Intel, BP, McDonald’s and Nestlé lost their jobs for less. None returned.
  
Why did NVIDIA cave? Three stark realities:
1. Too big to fire, or stay gone: With dozens of direct reports, handshake supply deals and no succession plan, the board had no viable exit.
2. Mutual dependency: Wall Street, Washington and the US AI world needed Huang to halt a trillion-dollar rout, yet Huang needed White House cover too.
3. Two-tier justice: One rule of law for billionaires, another for everyone else.
  
Where does this leave artificial intelligence and global compliance? 
• Board independence now looks negotiable when political and market pressure collide.  
• However, Federal, state and internal inquiries remain unfinished, the legal reckoning has not vanished.  
• Major AI buyers now have a governance reason, not just a cost one, to diversify beyond one founder.
  
NVIDIA got its founder back. The global AI sector just normalised a much steeper risk.
  
So, did NVIDIA’s board protect shareholders, or confirm that tech billionaires are above the rules?
  
#CorporateGovernance #ArtificialIntelligence #Leadership #NVIDIA

In sterile pharmaceutical manufacturing, sterility assurance cannot be established simply by obtaining satisfactory results in a sterility test.
It is the outcome of a well-designed, scientifically justified and consistently controlled manufacturing system.

True sterility assurance requires a holistic approach encompassing:
• Robust facility and equipment design
• Effective Contamination Control Strategy (CCS)
• Strong aseptic processing practices
• Personnel training, qualification and aseptic behaviour
• Effective environmental and process monitoring
• Robust sterilization and filtration processes
• Well-designed validation and qualification programmes
• A proactive Pharmaceutical Quality System (PQS)

Sterility assurance must be built into every stage of the manufacturing process, rather than relying on end-product testing to establish product sterility.

In my experience, the strength of a sterile manufacturing operation is reflected not merely in its ability to pass regulatory inspections, but in its ability to consistently identify, assess and control contamination risks.
Quality is not inspected into a product. It is built into the process.
Through SteriSure Consulting, I aim to support pharmaceutical manufacturers in strengthening quality systems, improving sterility assurance and fostering a culture of compliance through practical, science-based and risk-based approaches.

posts.title: "We're not an exchange, so we don't need FCA authorisation." I hear this a lot. The FCA's final perimeter guidance says it's often wrong.
posts.author: Shennind Awat-Ranai
posts.snippet:
"We're not an exchange, so we don't need FCA authorisation." I hear this a lot. The FCA's final perimeter guidance says it's often wrong.


PS26/18 landed on 16 September. It's the FCA's final guidance on what needs authorisation under the new regime.
  
Five things that catch founders out:
  
1.       Staking. Arranging qualifying cryptoasset staking is a regulated activity in its own right. Pure information or analytics probably isn't. Anything more hands-on might be.
  
2.       Lending and borrowing. Not standalone activities. But they get caught through the dealing, arranging or safeguarding around them. Most lending products have at least one.
  
3.       Custody is about control, not labels. Whether you're safeguarding turns on how much control you have over the assets. There's no express exclusion for "we're just the tech provider".
  
4.       Bundles. Services that add value aren't assessed one by one. Information-only services are unlikely to be arranging. Information plus execution is a different story.

5.      Offshore isn't a shield. Deal with UK consumers, or safeguard or stake for them, and you're treated as doing it in the UK. Unless an authorised person sits in between.

The guidance won't tell you whether you're in. The FCA says itself that it turns on 
the facts. That's the work.  

What this means for you: map every product feature against these five before you decide you're out of scope. If you're not sure which side of the perimeter you're on, my DMs are open.

#CryptoRegulation #FCA #Staking

posts.title: Europe has 450 million people and one legal framework.
posts.author: Piotr Słupski
posts.snippet:
Europe has 450 million people and one legal framework.

I pulled the full Y Combinator directory — 6,410 companies, every batch — filtered for frontier tech. Then I went looking for the money.

YC's hardtech share has nearly doubled in five years: 8.6% (2021) → 13.7% (2025) → 16.7% (2026).

Apollo Atomics — "the most compact nuclear reactors."
Atomarine — "floating nuclear powered data centers at sea."
Maritime Fusion — "fusion reactors for ships."
Latest batches: 126 US, 12 Europe.

2025 deep tech VC: US $144bn (+92%), Europe $20bn (+21%). Seven times, for 450 million people against America's 340.

Europe didn't lose the seed stage. Europe WON it. EU pre-seed + seed: $3.0bn. US: $2.7bn.
Growth stage: US $115bn, EU $28bn. Gap $87bn in one year.

The number I keep returning to. Late-stage VC from domestic investors: US 81%, EU 30%.

The exit is broken. The EU stock market is 55% of EU GDP; America's is 147%. And 70% of EU SMEs sell only at home — one in four exports to another EU state.

The EU's Quantum Flagship — announced to make Europe a global leader by 2030 — is €1bn over ten years. ~$113M a year. The US government spends ~$3.3bn a year on quantum.

Europe is running a 2030 world championship at 3% of the American budget. Target: ~100 error-corrected qubits by 2030. IBM shipped 400+ physical qubits a year ago.

Meanwhile Oxford Ionics, a British quantum champion, was bought by IonQ for $1.1bn.

Europe doesn't have a quantum problem. It has a keep-the-asset problem, and the price was set by someone else. When Computer Weekly summarised the EU's own deep tech plan this year: "European Union deep tech plan too late for quantum champions IQM and Pasqal." Too late — that's the operative word.

Gap to close: $87bn a year. New scale-up money: €5bn — coverage ~7%. The EIC's whole seven-year budget is one-eighth of a single year's gap.

Not stupidity — diagnosis. Intereconomics, the ECB and Dealroom all land on supply-side: pension architecture, bank-dominated finance, capital charges, 27 company laws, no exit market. Europe has ~$15tn in pension assets; 0.1% reaches venture. Europe isn't short of money. It's short of plumbing.

And one more thing. The Commission's own three KPIs: more startups, more centaurs, more unicorns. Not: more European-owned critical industrial layers. Score the ecosystem on company count and valuation and you optimise for building things someone else buys.

Legitimate — buyers make a lot of money. But a strategy that depends on being the buyer has already conceded the provider position.

The question isn't whether Europe can be the best buyer in the world. It's whether it intends to be one.

I build deeptech in Europe. So this isn't a complaint from outside. We have the scientists. We won the seed stage. We lose at scale — not because of paperwork. Because the exit is in Delaware and the pension money never shows up.

What would you add?

#DeepTech #Europe #VentureCapital #Quantum #Fusion #EIPolicy

La elaboración de un libro blanco de criptoactivos (White Paper) conforme al Reglamento MiCA requiere un análisis jurídico del token, el cumplimiento de las obligaciones de información y la adaptación del documento a los requisitos técnicos establecidos por ESMA.
 
Desde el 23 de diciembre de 2025, los White Papers sujetos a la obligación de presentación conforme a MiCA deben presentarse en formato XHTML con etiquetado iXBRL, utilizando la taxonomía desarrollada por ESMA.

Además, para los criptoactivos del título II de MiCA, el documento debe notificarse a la CNMV al menos 20 días hábiles antes de su publicación, sin que dicha notificación implique su aprobación por el supervisor.

En Data Bitlaw & Compliance hemos publicado una guía práctica en la que analizamos:

🔹 Cuándo es obligatorio elaborar un White Paper y qué excepciones contempla MiCA.
🔹 Las diferencias entre los regímenes aplicables a otros criptoactivos, ART y EMT.
🔹 Los requisitos de contenido y las obligaciones de información.
🔹 El procedimiento de notificación ante la CNMV.
🔹 Los requisitos técnicos de ESMA y el formato iXBRL.
🔹 Las obligaciones de modificación y actualización de los libros blancos.

📖 Puedes consultar nuestra guía práctica sobre White Papers MiCA en el primer comentario.

posts.title: "The smallest boundary that holds everything which matters.”
posts.author: Nicola Montefusco
posts.snippet:
"The smallest boundary that holds everything which matters.”

I am super glad to be sharing the third paper of the #concepteur series, "On #meanings and #value propositions", where I delve deeper into how we can define #innovation #strategies that force #organisation to commit.

The paper explains how to turn a shift in meaning into something a team can commit to and build.
It builds upon design research, from Roberto Verganti, Krippendorff and others, to describe how by #designing new meanings we can impact why people would choose aà products over another. Meaning becomes a #design #material, like form, materials and finish, and it deserves the same craft, care, and attention.

The tool I propose is called #conceptual value proposition: an #aesthetic line and its legend. A shift compressed into a #sentence short enough to be retold and guide the project strategy together with a legend that unfolds each word into what the organisation will actually do, who owns it and how it gets measured.
Inside the document you will find the way meanings migrate, the conceptual value proposition #grammar , and ways to test them.

There's also a section I hadn't planned but was prompted by Luca Mazzetti who asked me a simple question: how do we actually #train this mindset? The drafted answer became rituals, individual exercises, and deliberately human work.

The research is grounded in the literature and my own professional practice. The grammars and the tests are presented here as reasoning aids, not rigid and immutable instruments. 

That's why I started sharing these thought with you here and why I care about your #feedback, both privates and public. This inquiry, as any #cross-#contamination, was always meant to be built #together, and each next step will be better thanks to it.

Previous papers in the comments.

posts.title: South Korea's stablecoin rules, by the numbers.
posts.author: findeskasia
posts.snippet:
South Korea's stablecoin rules, by the numbers.
On 24 November, the Financial Services Commission (FSC) set out how it wants won-pegged stablecoins to work. The answer: banks stay in control, but tech firms keep a seat at the table.
The Bank of Korea had pushed for bank-majority issuers, warning that private stablecoins could be used to get around capital controls. The FSC proposal largely follows that line. It still needs to pass the National Assembly.
→ More than 50%: the combined stake banks must hold in any won stablecoin issuer
→ 5 billion won: the minimum capital an issuer needs
→ 100%: reserve backing for every token, with redemption on request and no interest paid
→ 20%: the cap on a major shareholder's stake in a crypto exchange (34% with approval), with three years to comply
Is a bank-majority model the right balance between stability and innovation, or will it slow fintechs down?
Full story in the first comment 👇
#FinDeskAsia #Fintech #SouthKorea #Stablecoins #Regulation #DigitalAssets #Payments
posts.reason: South Korea's stablecoin rules directly affect token classification and regulatory strategy; relevant to founders and GCs navigating MiCA-equivalent regimes, though not EU-focused.

comments.text: The bank-majority structure is a deliberate echo of how several EU member states are reading MiCAR's e-money token issuance requirements - control over the issuer, not just reserve backing, is becoming the common regulatory instinct globally for fiat-referenced tokens.

Does the three-year compliance window on the 20% exchange shareholder cap risk creating a wave of forced restructurings right as issuers are also trying to meet the capital threshold - which deadline do you think actually bites first?

We see the same tension in MiCAR ART and EMT authorisations - regulators want bank-grade control over issuance, but the capital and governance requirements often land hardest on exactly the tech firms best placed to build the product.

posts.title: A stablecoin could soon sit one tap away from a UAE current account. The status of the announcement is worth getting right.
posts.author: Rajini Gorantla
posts.snippet:
A stablecoin could soon sit one tap away from a UAE current account. The status of the announcement is worth getting right.

On 9 November, a major UAE bank’s digital banking arm announced a partnership to bring a dollar-backed stablecoin, registered with the Central Bank of the UAE, into its app. The token is issued under the CBUAE’s Payment Token Services Regulation, which requires registration, reserve management and ongoing attestations. A VARA-licensed infrastructure partner will provide liquidity and distribution, and the bank says it’s the first integration of a CBUAE-registered dollar stablecoin into a UAE digital bank. The bank’s app already offers crypto trading, launched in 2025, and serves close to half a million users.

Read the fine print. Reporting on the announcement describes it as a memorandum of understanding, with no trading start date and no customer eligibility terms yet. CBUAE rules also limit what registered foreign payment tokens can be used for: the token isn’t meant as a general-purpose payment method in the UAE, and its use is mainly tied to buying virtual assets.

That makes the story clearer. This isn’t a bank letting customers spend a stablecoin at a cafe. It’s a bank placing regulated dollar liquidity inside the same app where customers already manage money and trade digital assets.

Distribution, not issuance, is the prize. The firm that owns the customer’s everyday app can make a regulated token feel like a normal banking feature.

#Stablecoins #UAE #Banking #CBUAE #DigitalAssets #FinTech

Would you take a polygraph test to get a CEO role?

On recent visits to Ukrainian defence manufacturing companies, I have seen polygraph testing used in recruitment. When dev.ua asked seven defence-tech companies about their hiring this spring, six used polygraphs in some form. From mandatory testing for every candidate at Frontline Robotics to voluntary testing for sensitive roles at WIY. At Airlogix, it is a formal stage before an offer.

These companies operate in a country at war and face a constant threat of espionage and sabotage. Their caution is understandable. Polygraph screening also has a long history in US intelligence and federal law enforcement recruitment.

Executive search will run into this sooner rather than later. Airlogix now has a joint venture with Auterion producing drones in Germany, and cross-border recruitment of senior executives is likely to grow as Ukrainian and European defence industries integrate. In much of Europe, polygraph testing in recruitment raises employment law and data protection issues - its reliability is widely contested and most senior candidates will never have been asked to take one.

Screening requirements should be agreed with the client before the search is launched and explained to candidates early. Introducing a polygraph after three rounds of interviews risks losing an otherwise strong candidate. A Ukrainian employer hiring for a company in the EU may not be able to use the same screening as at home and that is worth clarifying before the search starts.

Have you come across this in a cross-border appointment? And would you take one yourself?

posts.title: *AI Career High Klaxon*
posts.author: Jude Copeland
posts.snippet:
*AI Career High Klaxon*

Practice Direction 06 of 2026 on AI in civil proceedings has just been published, taking effect on 6 January 2027, across civil matters before the Northern Ireland courts. 

This is a result of the work done by the AI Sub-Committee led by Humphreys J, of which I was a contributing member. 

I attach the Direction but, in summary:

 * Personal accountability does not move. Using AI does not shift or dilute responsibility for accuracy, propriety, or anything put before the court.

 * Checking another AI tool is not verification. Outputs have to be checked properly against real sources, especially for hallucinated cases, bad citations, and non-NI law.

 * Public AI tools are a major risk. Putting disclosed material, privileged communications, or sensitive personal data into public systems carries real risk.

 * Witness statements, affidavits, and expert reports have specific declaration wording. If AI plays a material part in drafting or assisting, you cannot treat it as a quiet shortcut.

 * Predictive coding is explicitly addressed. The Direction enables the use of predictive coding or technology-assisted review. (My personal view is that this has been underused in the jurisdiction, despite being established tech in GB.)

 * Sanctions. The court can look at costs, exclude evidence, strike out claims or defences, or refer conduct further if rules are ignored.

It will be important for practitioners, clients and experts to familiarise themselves with the requirements. 

Hopefully this Direction provides some clarity and guidance for the use of AI.

#CivilLitigation #AIRegulation #AIUseInCourt #AILeadership #EthicalAI

posts.author: Evie Breese
posts.snippet:
When I'm in labour and workers' rights circles, it can feel like the conversation hasn't caught up with the technology. When I'm in tech circles, I find myself asking: 'has anyone considered the workers here?' So, when I was invited to Westminster for the launch of Democratic Intelligence, which will explore how to put worker voice and democratic input at the heart of how AI is developed and deployed, I practically shouted 'now this is what I'm talking about!' ✨

It was a pleasure to hear from so many fantastic speakers, including Baroness Beeban Kidron, Isabelle Ferreras, Jeremias Adams-Prassl, Karl Koch, Catherine Bracy & Zarinah Agnew to name just a few. Under the Chatham House Rules I can't credit individual insights, but here are my key takeaways:

🗣️ Workers inside the frontier AI labs are the first line of defence and one of the only routes for internal accountability, governments must create the conditions for them to feel safe and heard to blow the whistle, BUT…

🗣️ We cannot rely on a few extraordinary people, facing extraordinary circumstances, to do extraordinary things. Whistleblowing cannot be the main mechanism for accountability. Dramatic change that uplifts worker voices and gives them a seat in governance are urgently needed.

🗣️AI is moving faster than democratic infrastructure can keep up with. In response, democratic capacity can be ramped up so that the public can feed into what good looks like, such as what constitutes a good/ bad AI model.

🗣️The constitutions published by frontier AI models - are they radical acts of intent, or simply PR? These constitutions often contain a mix of descriptions and aspirations, without signifying to the public which is which.

🗣️Just because the forms of technology are new, does not mean existing laws and rules of the game do not apply: a bias AI hiring system breaks the same rules as a bias HR manager.

🗣️It seems like almost everyone is BEGGING for AI regulation, but regulators remember: Big Tech companies like Meta and Amazon have such vast wealth that they can afford to comply with regulations that are likely to stifle start-ups, cementing their market dominance. 

Who else is working at the intersection of AI and work? Let's connect and compare notes 👀

posts.title: 128 countries just agreed to keep talking about "killer robots."
posts.author: Arastu Gupta
posts.snippet:
128 countries just agreed to keep talking about "killer robots."

That's the headline. The reality is more complicated. 

On November 21, 2026, at the UN conference in Geneva, the 128 states party to the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons wrapped up a week of negotiations on AI-powered weapons that can select and attack targets with little or no direct human control.

Here's what actually happened:

→ Nearly 100 countries backed negotiations on a legally binding ban on fully autonomous weapons
→ The US, one of the world's biggest military powers and AI pioneers, opposed a specific negotiating mandate. Russia also resisted
→ Diplomats couldn't agree on a mandate to negotiate a binding treaty
→ Instead, government experts will keep discussing elements of an agreement, with 2028 as the target

So, are killer robots banned? No.

There is no legally binding agreement. Countries have only agreed to continue the conversation. NGOs like Stop Killer Robots called the outcome "the lowest common denominator."

Why this matters 👇

The core question is simple but huge: should a machine ever decide to take a human life without meaningful human control?

This is no longer hypothetical. Autonomous systems are already moving onto battlefields, and AI is getting more capable every month. Regulation is moving at diplomatic speed. Technology is moving at startup speed.

What comes next?

2028 is the deadline to watch. If countries can't turn talks into a treaty by then, the technology will have set the rules before the law does.

For those of us in AI, defence tech and deep tech, this is the conversation that decides what responsible innovation looks like.

posts.snippet:
Scammers operate across an end-to-end attack lifecycle, yet most organizations still defend only their own isolated slice of the journey. 

As highlighted in a recent discussion on Deloitte Canada’s Full Circle podcast featuring Anthony Ostler (President and CEO of the Canadian Bankers’ Association) and host Hilary Doyle, closing that visibility gap requires shifting from siloed institutional defenses to a deeply connected, cross-sector ecosystem.

While a fraudster tracks a victim seamlessly from a social media ad or spoofed SMS, through an encrypted messaging app, and finally onto banking or crypto rails, individual organizations typically see only a single disconnected signal. Without shared intelligence across telecommunications, social platforms, financial institutions, and law enforcement, criminal networks exploit the blind spots between sectors to move money before anyone connects the dots.

Key Takeaways on Building a Connected Fraud Defense

👉 Closing the cross-sector visibility gap: Banks often see the final payment instruction, while telecom providers see the spoofed call and tech platforms see the initial lure. Breaking down operational and regulatory silos to share real-time threat signals across industries allows defenders to disrupt scams upstream before funds ever leave an account. 

👉 Designing controls around the human journey: Traditional fraud rules focus heavily on technical transaction anomalies, overlooking how psychological manipulation unfolds over days or weeks. 
Designing friction and interventions around how victims actually experience scams, such as dynamic behavioral prompts during high-risk transfers creates far more effective protection. 

👉 Public-private partnerships as a force multiplier: Dismantling organized fraud syndicates requires coordinated governance between banks, regulators, technology providers, and law enforcement to follow the money across borders and freeze mule networks in real time.
